lead: Stereolithography is an additive process that builds a part from a liquid photopolymer. A UV laser or projector draws one cross-section on the resin surface. Where the light falls, the resin cures into a thin solid layer. The platform then moves down by one layer thickness, a blade spreads fresh resin, and the next cross-section is drawn. Supports hold overhangs. After building, the part is cleaned and post-cured. It is used for detailed prototypes, dental models, jewellery patterns and transparent parts. Some syllabi call the machine stereolithography apparatus, SLA.
prereq: You need: the AM process chain from Chapter 7.2 and the basic idea that a photopolymer liquid hardens when UV light strikes it.

blocks.text: Stereolithography is a vat photopolymerisation process. A vat is a tank of liquid photopolymer: a resin made of monomers, oligomers and a photoinitiator. The photoinitiator absorbs UV light and starts a chain reaction that turns the liquid into a solid polymer network. The build platform starts just below the resin surface, leaving a thin gap. A UV laser is focused to a small spot and steered by a pair of small motor-driven mirrors, called galvanometer mirrors. The mirrors move the beam along the cross-section of one layer. Only the scanned area cures; the rest stays liquid. The first layer sticks to the platform. The platform then moves down by one layer thickness and a recoating blade, also called a wiper, spreads a fresh film of resin over the cured layer. The next cross-section is scanned and bonds to the previous layer. This repeats until the part is complete.

A projector-based machine, often called digital light processing, flashes a whole layer at once through a mask. The layer-by-layer logic is the same. The cured part is lifted off, drained, washed in solvent, supports are removed, and it is post-cured under strong UV to finish the polymer network.

items: Lower the platform to leave a thin resin gap above the previous layer.
Scan the layer cross-section with the UV beam, or project the full layer image.
Let the exposed resin cure and bond to the layer below.
Move the platform down by one layer thickness.
Spread fresh resin with the recoating blade.
Repeat, then drain, clean, remove supports and post-cure.

blocks.text: The main machine parts are the UV laser or projector, the galvanometer scan head, the focusing lens, the resin vat, the build platform, the recoating blade and the control software. The scan head moves the laser spot quickly, so the beam can trace fine borders and hatch lines. Hatch spacing is the distance between neighbouring scan lines; it must be small enough that the cured lines join. The spot size and layer thickness set the resolution, the smallest detail the machine can hold. Thin layers give smoother surfaces and finer detail but take longer because there are more layers.

blocks.where: N is the number of layers, H is the part height in mm, and t is the layer thickness in mm.

items: Standard resin: rigid and clear; for visual prototypes.
Tough or ABS-like resin: better impact strength; for snap fits and casings.
Flexible resin: rubber-like; for gaskets and grips.
Castable resin: burns out cleanly; for jewellery and investment casting patterns.
Dental and medical resins: tooth models, surgical guides and hearing-aid shells.

blocks.text: SLA is not selective laser sintering. SLS uses a powder bed and a laser that sinters thermoplastic powder; SLA uses a liquid resin that cures by chemical reaction. Do not write one for the other in an exam; see Chapter 7.5 for SLS. SLA parts are accurate and smooth, but they are weaker than moulded or metal parts and can creep under load. Hollow parts need drain holes.

Supports are thin pillars built from the platform or from the part up to an overhang. They carry the overhang while it is still soft and stop it bending. Supports are removed after building, so they leave small marks. The part is drained, washed in solvent such as isopropyl alcohol to remove uncured resin, and post-cured under UV. Post-cure raises strength and stability but can also cause slight shrinkage. Designers allow for this by testing a small coupon first.

Accuracy is affected by spot size, layer thickness, resin shrinkage, and the depth of cure. If the laser gives too much energy, the cured line becomes wider than the scan path, a condition called overcure; it can fill fine gaps. Too little energy leaves tacky, weak layers. Build orientation matters: a flat face parallel to the platform is smooth, but a steep overhang needs more supports.

SLA is used for form-and-fit models, master patterns for investment casting, dental aligners and surgical guides, jewellery, transparent fluid-flow models, and small production parts when the resin suits the duty.

examples.question: A stereolithography part is 30 mm tall and is built with layers 0.1 mm thick. The hatch length, the total scan path in one layer, is 4,000 mm. The laser scan speed is 500 mm/s. Find the number of layers, the scan time for one layer, the total scan time, and the scan time in minutes. Ignore recoating and post-cure in the scan time.
steps: Number of layers: N = H / t = 30 mm / 0.1 mm = 300 layers.
Scan time for one layer: t<sub>layer</sub> = L / v = 4,000 mm / 500 mm/s = 8 s.
Total scan time: T<sub>scan</sub> = N × t<sub>layer</sub> = 300 × 8 s = 2,400 s.
Convert to minutes: T<sub>scan</sub> = 2,400 s / 60 s/min = 40 min.
examples.answer: The part has 300 layers, each layer takes 8 s, and the total scan time is 2,400 s, which is 40 min; the real build also needs recoating and post-cure time.
examples.check:
H = 30.0
layer = 0.1
hatch = 4000.0
speed = 500.0
N = H / layer
t_layer = hatch / speed
T = N * t_layer
print(int(N))
print(int(t_layer))
print(int(T))
print(int(T / 60))

traps: SLA uses a liquid photopolymer, not a thermoplastic filament; the laser cures only the scanned area, and overhangs need supports.
SLA is vat photopolymerisation; SLS is powder bed fusion. SLS sinters powder, SLA cures resin. Mixing the names loses marks.
The layer time is hatch length divided by scan speed, not layer thickness divided by scan speed. Keep millimetres with millimetres and seconds with seconds.
Post-cure is a separate UV step after cleaning; it is not part of the layer scan time. Recoating, lifting and draining also add to the total build time.
Projector or DLP stereolithography cures a full layer image at once, but it is still a layer-by-layer vat process, not material jetting.

quiz.q: What kind of material does stereolithography cure, and what energy source starts the cure?
quiz.a: A liquid photopolymer resin; UV light from a laser or projector starts the cure.

quiz.q: Why does an SLA part with an overhang need supports?
quiz.a: The overhang is built over liquid resin, so it has nothing solid below it. Supports hold it while it is soft and stop it bending or collapsing.

quiz.q: A part is 50 mm tall with 0.05 mm layers. Each layer has hatch length 3,000 mm and scan speed 600 mm/s. Find the layer count, time per layer, and total scan time in seconds and minutes.
Why does SLA usually give a smoother surface than FDM?
quiz.a: SLA cures liquid resin with a small spot in thin layers, so there is no extruded filament bead or nozzle raster. The surface follows the fine scan and layer steps; support marks and layer lines remain.

quiz.q: State two differences between SLA and SLS.
quiz.a: SLA uses liquid photopolymer cured by UV; SLS uses thermoplastic powder sintered by a laser. SLA needs supports; SLS is supported by the powder bed.

quiz.q: Name two post-processing steps for an SLA part.
quiz.a: Drain and wash off uncured resin; remove supports; post-cure under UV. Any two.

quiz.q: If layer thickness is doubled while hatch length and scan speed stay the same, what happens to layer count and scan time?
quiz.a: Layer count halves because N = H / t. Scan time halves because each layer has the same hatch length and there are half as many layers. Surface finish becomes rougher.

beyond: Not for the exam. Research machines use micro-stereolithography and two-photon curing to make features smaller than a hair. Projector and LCD masked systems cure a whole layer in one flash for faster dental and hearing-aid production. Bioresins and hydrogels are being tested for tissue scaffolds. Search for vat photopolymerisation, DLP stereolithography, two-photon polymerisation and biocompatible SLA resins.
